title: Replicas Shards and Safe Evolution
description: Compare read replicas, sharding, partition pruning, hot keys, compatible backfills, and cache invalidation through practical consistency and scaling labs.

questions.question_text: What should precede a scaling topology decision?
options: A measured bottleneck and behavior requirement
questions.explanation: The solution must address the actual limiting resource and contract.

questions.question_text: What can a read replica offload?
questions.explanation: Replicas can add read capacity under an explicit consistency policy.

questions.question_text: Why can a confirmation read show an old value?
options: A successful write must always be lost
questions.explanation: Read routing and freshness can differ from the authoritative write path.

questions.question_text: Why is a fixed sleep not proof a replica caught up?
options: Lag can vary and exceed the delay
questions.explanation: Timing guesses do not establish a replication boundary.

questions.question_text: What does sharding distribute?
questions.explanation: Shards own subsets of data and introduce routing boundaries.

questions.question_text: What must cross-shard business uniqueness address explicitly?
options: Coordination or another supported enforcement design
questions.explanation: Independent databases do not automatically enforce a global relation.

questions.question_text: Why can a hot campus remain a bottleneck after tenant sharding?
options: Every campus must have equal traffic
Its workload still routes to one shard
questions.explanation: A skewed key can concentrate load despite more shards.

questions.question_text: What does partition pruning avoid?
options: Partitions that cannot contain qualifying rows
questions.explanation: Recognized predicates can exclude irrelevant partitions.

questions.question_text: Is partitioning automatically multi-server sharding?
options: Only when a table has rows
questions.explanation: Partitioning and independent ownership distribution are distinct.

questions.question_text: Why include happened_on in the example MySQL primary key?
options: Partition unique-key rules require the partition column
questions.explanation: The example respects the relevant partition key inclusion restriction.

questions.question_text: What uniqueness is not established by PRIMARY KEY(event_id, happened_on)?
questions.explanation: A composite key does not imply uniqueness of each component alone.

questions.question_text: Why is dropping a populated partition sensitive?
questions.explanation: Partition removal can be a data deletion operation.

questions.question_text: What is needed during overlapping application versions?
options: Immediate removal of all old fields
questions.explanation: Schema evolution must consider old and new callers together.

questions.question_text: Why should backfills use bounded restartable progress?
options: Failures and resource use need controlled recovery
questions.explanation: Batching and checkpoints support manageable work and restart.

questions.question_text: What race must a backfill design consider?
options: A concurrent newer write to the same value
questions.explanation: A backfill must not overwrite legitimate newer state incorrectly.

questions.question_text: What must cache keys include?
options: Dimensions affecting result and access scope
Only the last digit of an ID
questions.explanation: Incomplete keys can mix values or permission scopes.

questions.question_text: Does a short cache TTL guarantee read-your-writes?
questions.explanation: Expiration bounds some staleness but does not establish immediate consistency.

questions.question_text: Why can invalidation alone race with readers?
options: A reader may repopulate an older value
questions.explanation: Cache population and source writes need a failure-aware design.

questions.question_text: What evidence is stronger than a backfill script merely finishing?
options: A screenshot of a terminal prompt
questions.explanation: Successful process exit alone does not prove data correctness.

questions.question_text: What do these scaling labs not establish?
options: A deployed topology or exercised failover
The distinction between partitions and shards
questions.explanation: Operational claims require actual deployment and drill evidence.

notes:
## Identify the resource that limits the workload

A campus platform becomes slow when registration opens. It is tempting to announce that the database needs sharding, but the symptom could come from an expensive report, a hot row, exhausted connections, insufficient I/O capacity, or an application retry storm. Scaling begins with a measured bottleneck and a required behavior. Record latency, throughput, error rates, workload mix, and resource observations before choosing a new topology. More servers do not correct an invalid transaction or an unbounded query.

Separate read capacity, write capacity, data volume, and availability goals. A read replica can offload eligible reads while leaving one primary write bottleneck. Partitioning can reduce scanned data for suitable predicates without distributing a table across independent database servers. Sharding distributes ownership across databases but introduces routing and cross-shard complexity. These tools address different constraints and can be combined only with an explicit consistency and operational design.

## Read replicas require a freshness contract

A replica receives changes from another database according to the replication system. Replication can lag, so a read routed immediately after a successful write may observe an older state. For a profile edit confirmation, that can look like a lost update even though the primary committed correctly. Define which reads require recent writes and which reports tolerate bounded staleness. Routing is part of the user-visible contract.

One practical policy keeps a transaction and its immediate verification reads on the authoritative write path. Other policies use a supported replication position or consistency mechanism. Exact mechanisms depend on the engine and topology. A fixed arbitrary sleep is not a reliable proof that a replica has caught up. Under failure or heavy load, the delay can exceed the guessed interval.

Replicas also need capacity and operational monitoring. Sending every expensive analytical query to one replica can overload it and increase lag. A failover candidate may have a different role from a disposable reporting replica. Document promotion procedures, connection routing, and what acknowledged work can be lost under the chosen replication mode. These are operational properties that require real drills rather than a topology drawing alone.

## Sharding changes data ownership

Sharding assigns subsets of records to independent database owners using a routing key. A campus identifier is a possible key when most operations belong to one campus, but suitability depends on actual access patterns and distribution. A cross-campus report may need multiple shards. A globally unique business constraint may require an explicit coordination mechanism. Foreign keys cannot simply be assumed to enforce relationships across independent databases.

A shard map or deterministic routing rule must be stable and reviewable. Moving a campus between shards needs a controlled ownership transition so requests do not write to both places or miss recently moved data. Retry handling and idempotent operations remain important, because a timeout does not prove a write failed. Sharding is a change to transaction and failure boundaries, not merely adding a WHERE campus_id clause.

Hot keys can remain hot after sharding. If one campus supplies most writes, routing all its records to one shard leaves that shard overloaded. Subdividing by another key can spread load but may make campus-level transactions and reports more expensive. Measure skew and evaluate the operations that must remain atomic. A balanced count of tenants is not evidence of a balanced workload.

## Partition pruning needs a matching predicate

Table partitioning separates a table into engine-managed partitions according to a rule. Pruning avoids considering partitions that cannot contain qualifying rows. A monthly date partition can help a bounded date query when the engine recognizes the predicate. It does not make a query over the entire history free, and it does not automatically distribute the table across independent machines.

```sql
CREATE TABLE event_archive (
 event_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
 happened_on DATE NOT NULL,
 campus_id INT NOT NULL,
 PRIMARY KEY(event_id,happened_on)
)
PARTITION BY RANGE COLUMNS(happened_on) (
 PARTITION p_before_feb VALUES LESS THAN ('2026-02-01'),
 PARTITION p_feb VALUES LESS THAN ('2026-03-01'),
 PARTITION p_future VALUES LESS THAN (MAXVALUE)
);
EXPLAIN SELECT event_id,happened_on FROM event_archive
WHERE happened_on >= '2026-02-01'
 AND happened_on < '2026-03-01';
```

This MySQL teaching definition includes the partition column in the primary key, following the relevant unique-key restriction. It does not establish that event_id alone is globally unique. That distinction matters if the application previously depended on that exact uniqueness rule. The expected inspection is that the plan can identify eligible partitions for this interval; no actual plan output or pruning result is claimed here.

Adding partitions also creates lifecycle work. Future ranges must be available before new data arrives, and retention changes require explicit data authorization. Never treat partition removal as harmless maintenance: removing a populated partition can delete real data. Test boundaries exactly on partition transitions and review the actual engine restrictions before proposing production DDL.

## Evolve schemas and backfill deliberately

An online change should preserve compatibility while old and new application versions overlap. A common pattern introduces a compatible new representation, backfills existing rows in bounded batches, switches readers after verification, and later retires the old representation under separate approval. The details depend on the change and engine behavior. Calling DDL online does not guarantee zero locks, zero resource cost, or safe execution under every workload.

Backfills need stable progress and restart behavior. Batch by a suitable key, avoid unbounded transactions, and record which range has been processed. Concurrent writes can race with backfill updates, so define which value wins and how new writes populate the new representation. Verify completeness and consistency before changing the authoritative read path. A script finishing without an exception is weaker evidence than a reconciled result.

A compatibility rollback must also account for writes made after the switch. Restoring old application code does not automatically restore an obsolete representation that stopped receiving updates. Define whether both representations remain maintained during the rollback window and verify that assumption with failure tests.

## Cache invalidation is a consistency design

A cache can reduce repeated database reads, but cached entries must expire or be invalidated according to the product's freshness needs. Cache keys must include the dimensions that affect the result, such as campus, user scope, filter, or version. Omitting a permission scope can become a data exposure, not merely a stale display. Keep authorization enforcement on the trusted path.

Invalidation and writes can race. A reader may repopulate an old value after a writer removes the cache entry. Versioned values, supported transaction/event publication patterns, or bounded expiration can address different requirements, but each needs a failure model. Avoid claiming that a short time to live guarantees read-your-writes or resolves every race. Cache behavior must be tested alongside source ownership and retry policy.

## Worked lab: route a confirmation read

A student changes a profile value, receives success, then sees the old value. The solution traces the write destination, the read destination, and replication or cache freshness. Check the committed authoritative value before repeating the write. If the product requires immediate confirmation, route that verification through a mechanism that meets the freshness contract. Do not declare data loss merely from one stale read.

A second lab models a hot campus with eighty percent of writes. A four-shard plan assigning one quarter of campuses to each shard can still leave one shard overloaded. The solution uses workload weights and transaction boundaries, rather than tenant counts alone, to evaluate routing. Explain the added complexity if the hot campus is subdivided.

## Worked lab: verify an evolution checkpoint

A new normalized display field is backfilled in batches. The solved checklist compares missing values, mismatched derivations, boundary keys, and concurrent updates before switching readers. Test restart after a failed batch and confirm repeated processing does not corrupt newer writes. This is a design lab with a required execution test plan, rather than a claim that a migration has run.

Continue with [Query Plans and Cardinality Lab](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/query-plans-and-cardinality-lab) before distributing avoidable query work, and [View Maintenance](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/view-maintenance) for freshness and reconciliation concepts. This lesson introduces scaling decisions without claiming a deployed topology or a complete operational runbook.
